entry.title: [Open Agricola Development Diary] EP 1: Why Rebuild Agricola?
entry.summary:
Agricola is more than a decade old. By today’s standards, it is not especially heavy. How hard could a complete digital version really be?

Its rulebook is not frighteningly thick. The trouble is that a lot of traps can fit inside one sentence. Take Hammer Crusher:

Immediately before you renovate to stone, you get 2 clay and 1 reed and you can take a “Build Rooms” action.

I glanced at that text and thought: what is so hard about this? Hand out the resources, let the player build, done. Once a program has to run it, the questions arrive immediately. Exactly when does it trigger? Can someone who cannot yet afford a stone renovation choose Renovation in the first place? How many more traps can you spot? I spotted none the first time. I will come back to them later.

This afternoon, I made the first commit to Open Agricola. Before I started, my thoughts kept returning to the card that had already caused me so much pain.

entry.title: Notes on Compression Algorithms
entry.summary:
Know how to solve every problem that has been solved.

What I cannot create I do not understand.

–Richard P. Feynman

An internal competition at work forced me to learn several compression algorithms within a short time last month. I also implemented some of them, including lz77, deflate, bwt, and bcm. You never know until you practice: the moment you begin writing code, you discover that some things you thought you understood were never truly understood. I also recently watched a series of videos about the late physicist Richard Feynman. One detail left a deep impression. After his death, people found that he had preserved the two sentences above in the upper-left corner of his office blackboard, where they would not be erased accidentally.

From a young age, Feynman’s father taught him that knowing and understanding were two different things. He therefore retained the curiosity to think through every problem.
The two sentences express essentially the same idea: only when you can create something yourself do you truly understand it. Reaching that point requires knowing how every problem was actually solved, not merely remembering a conclusion. The highest level of understanding a concept is being able to teach it to somebody else.

Inspired by that idea, I wrote this article to record my recent exploration of compression algorithms.

entry.title: [A Life in Board Games] Episode 7: The Art and Way of Agricola
entry.summary:
The Trough of Fatigue

Time is always the greatest enemy. No matter how deeply we once loved something, we have to admit that fatigue eventually arrives. What reaches an extreme must reverse; what flourishes must decline. In one sense, my love for something feels a little like this technology maturity curve.

As time passes, a board gamer’s enthusiasm for the hobby follows roughly the same curve. At first, everything looks fresh and the newcomer frantically chases new releases. Then passion gradually cools. Current designs begin to reveal familiar patterns, and every new game recalls some old classic. A trough follows, when fewer and fewer games seem genuinely fun. Yet only after passing through that process and washing away the glitter is a player willing to look back at older games: classics that were never explored deeply during the frantic pursuit of novelty—such as Agricola. So today, let us properly discuss this former titan of the board-game world.

Agricola is a standard Eurogame that demands both short-term decisions and long-term strategy, and it excels at both. As in every traditional abstract strategy game, the outcome is theoretically determined from the beginning; there are simply too many game states for even a computer to calculate every decision. That does not prevent generation after generation of masters from continuing to explore their craft—although AlphaGo recently dealt humanity a heavy blow. Agricola is not a traditional abstract game. It contains randomness and hidden information, but limits both so that replayability increases without allowing the system to escape control. One might say it preserves the soul of the Eurogame as fully as possible.

entry.title: titanxxh's 2016 Board Game Review
entry.summary:
BG Stats

The BG Stats app records board-game sessions and provides statistics, making it the perfect assistant for an annual review.

Across 2016, I played 105 different games, a number that surprised even me. BG Stats currently does not recognize relationships between base games and expansions very well, however, counting non-standalone expansions as separate games. That is annoying, though I rarely play with expansions, so this figure should remain fairly accurate. My H-index was only 6, meaning just six games reached six plays, so the 2016 10 × 10 Challenge definitively failed again. There are simply too many new games these days. BGG’s database grows by almost 10,000+ titles every year, the number of halls at Essen increases annually, and chasing new releases is a consensus within my gaming circle—yes, President Wen, I mean you. Combined with the drastic loss of free time after beginning full-time work, these factors have made repeated plays increasingly rare. I miss my university years, when we could play Ora et Labora dozens of times.

Breaking the numbers down, I played 158 sessions during the first four months, before starting the job, though online Agricola accounted for a large share. After I joined the company, only 35 percent of the year’s plays remained; May and September both recorded zero sessions… This will probably deteriorate further in 2017, so instead of another 10 × 10 Challenge, I plan to attempt 100 × 1. After Club A stopped hosting open events, I never had a fixed venue. Chengshan Road now looks likely to become the place I visit most often, mainly because it is close to both E and me. As a standard Eurogamer, more than half my plays were at four players, demonstrating just how deeply the common overseas family structure of two parents and two children has influenced German-style games.

E, Bowl King, and the Editor-in-Chief became my best gaming buddies this year—last year it was Xiaoda, E, and Bowl King. I thank them for their company, especially the Editor-in-Chief, who read the rules alone and taught us T.I.M.E Stories and Pandemic Legacy. Sadly, after I stopped going to Club A, I never saw the Editor-in-Chief again T_T… Bowl King left to study in Hong Kong, so I barely saw him during the second half of the year. E was probably still the person I met most often. In a year without a regular venue, we even held one session inside Ctrip’s headquarters and visited the legendary senior executive’s office—the one whose routine is running at work and playing with his child after work. I also thank all our other friends and everyone on the editorial team. I even saw C this year, although she is really E’s fan…

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 8. ...and then, we held hands: Overview, Unboxing, and Review
entry.summary:
Game Overview

…and then, we held hands, which we simply call “Holding Hands,” is a nonverbal cooperative game for two players. Their goal is to save a relationship on the verge of collapse. Each player’s perspective changes continuously with their position, and the pair must cooperate to balance both their inner emotions and their shared relationship, repairing the rift between them.

Players complete a sequence of objectives by ending their turns on the corresponding nodes. Once every objective is complete, both must enter the central ring together to achieve final victory.

Players may not discuss the game itself. Each must independently consider both their own cards and their partner’s, anticipate possible movement, and avoid trapping either player and losing the game. Conversation unrelated to the game is allowed. For an additional challenge, the entire game can be played in complete silence.

entry.title: Touring a City Alone
entry.summary:
With full-time work about to begin, I slipped away to Beijing alone last week. I had wanted to explore the capital properly ever since attending a conference there the previous year. My only earlier visit had been when I was too young to remember anything, while last year’s schedule was so limited that I visited only the Forbidden City and the National Museum of China. As my final chance to relax before starting work, traveling alone felt free and pleasant.

entry.title: [titanxxh's Essen 2015] 7. Signorie Overview and Review
entry.summary:
Introduction

Fifteenth-century Italy was a great land, but also one filled with intrigue. Its chaotic political environment gave rise to a new form of government—the signoria—while many ambitious noble families grew steadily stronger.
After years of maneuvering in the shadows, their moment finally arrived. It was their turn to control the cities and shape Italy’s future; their stories would enter the history books.

In Signorie, each player represents a noble power. You are lord of a celebrated Renaissance family, increasing your influence and building a mighty dynasty by arranging marriages with six of the most prestigious houses.

You must choose your children’s destinies wisely. Give the men of your family one of three forms of training—military, religious, or political—then send them on diplomatic missions to the right cities at the right time, or strategically arrange political marriages for them.

At the beginning of each round, roll twenty dice in five colors. Players take turns choosing a die from the common area. Its color determines the action available, while its number indicates the discount on that action. Hiring assistants improves the efficiency of a player’s actions.
The dice mechanism is simple yet somewhat innovative. Each player can take at most four actions per round. Money is always tight, so high-numbered dice are tempting, but their values require careful trade-offs: a player whose total exceeds 13 loses the round’s reward.

The player with the most Influence at the end wins.
